groups.title: Unit Testing with Vitest
groups.question: Explain how you write fast, focused unit tests for a Node.js service.

followUps.Vitest Fundamentals & Test Structure: What kinds of bugs do unit tests catch that integration tests often miss?
followUps.Mocking with vi.mock & vi.spyOn: When would you use vi.spyOn instead of calling the real dependency in a test?

evidence.text: Unit tests check one function or module alone, so they're fast and point straight at the broken logic.
They're good for catching logic bugs and edge cases, like empty input or boundaries, that integration tests rarely try.

notEnough: Only saying unit tests test small pieces without saying what bugs they catch.

evidence.text: vi.spyOn wraps a real function so the test can check how it was called, and optionally replace its result.
vi.mock replaces a whole module, for example to fake an HTTP client or a payment service.
You fake dependencies that are slow, costly or unpredictable, so the test only checks your own logic.

notEnough: Only naming vi.mock and vi.spyOn without explaining when to use them.

groups.title: Integration Testing
groups.question: Walk through how you test a Fastify API end to end against a real database.

followUps.API Testing with Supertest & Fastify inj: What kinds of bugs does an inject() integration test catch that unit tests miss?
followUps.Test Databases & Fixtures: Why should each test suite own an isolated database instead of sharing a dev database?

evidence.text: Fastify's inject() sends a fake HTTP request through the whole app without opening a network port.
It catches bugs between the parts: wrong routes, missing auth, validation and serialization mistakes, and wrong status codes.

notEnough: Only saying test the API with inject without saying what it catches.

evidence.text: Each test suite gets its own database or schema, reset between tests with known fixture data.
A shared dev database has unpredictable data and tests that interfere with each other, which makes results flaky.

notEnough: Only saying use a test database without explaining isolation.

groups.title: Coverage & CI
groups.question: Explain how you use coverage and CI to keep a test suite trustworthy over time.

followUps.Coverage with V8 & Istanbul: Why can a high line coverage number still hide untested bugs?
followUps.Testing in CI with GitHub Actions: Why would you run your CI tests against more than one Node.js version?

evidence.text: Coverage reports which lines and branches ran during the tests.
A line can run without its result being checked, so high coverage can still hide bugs.
Coverage is useful to find untested code, not to prove the code works.

notEnough: Only saying aim for high coverage without explaining its limits.

misconceptions.text: Says 100% coverage proves the code has no bugs.

evidence.text: CI runs the tests automatically on every push or pull request.
A version matrix runs them on several Node versions, catching code that only breaks on one of them before users or upgrades hit it.

notEnough: Only saying run tests in CI without explaining the version matrix.

groups.title: Test Patterns
groups.question: Explain how you write tests that stay readable and catch breaking API changes.

followUps.Arrange-Act-Assert Pattern: How does the Arrange-Act-Assert structure make a failing test easier to understand?
followUps.Contract Testing: What kind of production breakage does contract testing prevent?

evidence.text: Each test is split into arrange (set up data), act (run the code) and assert (check the result).
When it fails, you can see at once what was set up, what was called and what was expected.

notEnough: Only naming the three parts without explaining why it helps.

evidence.text: A contract test checks that the provider API still matches what its consumers expect: fields, types and status codes.
It catches breaking API changes, like a renamed field, before deploy instead of in production.

notEnough: Only saying contract testing tests APIs without explaining what breakage it prevents.
